articleHeader.title: Python File Handling — open(), read(), and write() Explained Properly
articleHeader.subtitle: Everything you actually need to know about working with files in Python — open(), file modes, the with statement and why it matters, reading and writing text, CSV, and JSON, and the exact FileNotFoundError you'll hit while learning this.

sections.title: What is File Handling in Python?

blocks.text: File handling is how a Python program reads data from files on disk, writes data back out to them, and manages everything in between — creating new files, appending to existing ones, and, critically, closing them properly when you're done. Almost every real program eventually needs this: reading a configuration file, saving user data, processing a CSV export, logging errors to a text file. Python's built-in open() function is the single entry point for essentially all of it.

The basic shape looks almost deceptively simple: f = open("data.txt", "r") opens a file for reading, f.read() pulls its entire contents into a string, and f.close() releases the file. Three lines, done. But that simplicity hides a genuine trap: if anything goes wrong between opening and closing — an exception gets raised, a return statement exits the function early — f.close() never runs, and the file stays open longer than it should, potentially locking other programs out of it or leaking a file descriptor your operating system eventually runs out of if it happens enough times.

This is exactly the problem the with statement was built to solve, and it's the single most important habit this entire topic teaches: with open("data.txt", "r") as f: guarantees the file gets closed automatically the moment that block ends, whether it ends normally or because of an error. I genuinely don't write open() without with anymore, for anything, and once you understand exactly why, you probably won't either — it's not a stylistic preference, it's a correctness guarantee that manual close() calls simply can't match.

This guide covers open() and its file modes precisely, why with genuinely matters (not just as a best practice, but mechanically), the different ways to read and write content, working with CSV and JSON files using the standard library, text encoding, and the specific FileNotFoundError traceback that every Python developer eventually hits.

sections.title: History — How Python's File Handling Evolved

blocks.text: File I/O has been core to Python since its earliest releases, but the specific mechanisms for doing it safely and correctly have genuinely improved over the language's history.

items.text: — The open() built-in function was present from Python's earliest public release, providing basic file reading and writing capability modelled conceptually on C's file I/O functions.

items.strong: Early Python — Manual close() Was the Only Option
items.text: — Before context managers existed, every file had to be closed manually with f.close(), and a genuine, common bug pattern was forgetting to close a file, or failing to close it when an exception occurred partway through processing.

— Introduced the with statement and the broader context manager protocol (__enter__ and __exit__ methods), giving Python a general-purpose mechanism for guaranteed setup/cleanup — file handling became its single most common and immediately obvious use case.

— Made a fundamental, sometimes-confusing-at-first change: files opened in text mode now return str objects (proper Unicode text) by default, while binary mode ('rb', 'wb') returns bytes objects — a genuine, deliberate split that Python 2 handled far less strictly.

— Reorganised Python's built-in exception hierarchy for OS-related errors, consolidating several separate exceptions into a cleaner structure — FileNotFoundError became a distinct, specific subclass of the broader OSError, rather than a generic IOError with a matching error number.

— The pathlib module, introduced in Python 3.4, matured into the recommended, object-oriented way to handle file paths, offering a cleaner alternative to string-based path manipulation via the older os.path module, while open() itself remained the standard tool for actual file content I/O.

— open() combined with the with statement remains the standard, expected way to handle files in Python. pathlib.Path objects are increasingly common for path manipulation, and both integrate cleanly — Path objects even have their own .open() method that behaves identically to the built-in function.

sections.title: Key Characteristics of Python File Handling

blocks.text: Here are the 11 things worth knowing precisely about how file handling actually works in Python:

items.title: open() Is the Universal Entry Point
items.text: Every file operation starts with open(filepath, mode), returning a file object that supports reading, writing, or both, depending on the mode string passed.

items.title: Mode Strings Control Behaviour
items.text: 'r' for read, 'w' for write (overwrites existing content), 'a' for append, 'x' for exclusive creation (fails if the file exists), and 'b' appended to any of these switches to binary mode instead of text mode.

items.title: with Guarantees Cleanup
items.text: The with statement ensures a file's close() method runs automatically when the block exits, even if an exception occurs partway through — this is a genuine correctness guarantee, not just tidier syntax.

items.title: Multiple Ways to Read Content
items.text: .read() pulls the entire file as one string, .readline() reads a single line, .readlines() returns all lines as a list, and iterating directly over the file object (for line in f:) reads it lazily, one line at a time.

items.title: write() Doesn't Add Newlines Automatically
items.text: Unlike print(), f.write() does NOT append a newline character automatically — writing multiple lines requires explicitly including \n in each call, or writing pre-joined multi-line text.

items.title: Files Have a Cursor Position
items.text: Reading or writing advances an internal position marker within the file. f.tell() reports the current position, and f.seek(offset) moves it, letting you re-read from the beginning or jump to a specific byte.

items.title: Text Mode vs Binary Mode
items.text: Text mode ('r', 'w') automatically decodes bytes to str using a specified or platform-default encoding. Binary mode ('rb', 'wb') returns raw bytes objects with no decoding at all — required for images, executables, and other non-text files.

items.title: Encoding Should Be Explicit
items.text: open(path, 'r', encoding='utf-8') explicitly sets the text encoding. Omitting it relies on the platform's default encoding, which can genuinely differ between operating systems and cause subtle, hard-to-reproduce bugs.

items.title: FileNotFoundError on a Missing File
items.text: Attempting to open a nonexistent file in read mode ('r') raises FileNotFoundError immediately, with the exact filename included in the error message.

items.title: Standard Library Modules for Structured Files
items.text: The csv module handles comma-separated files correctly (including edge cases like commas inside quoted fields), and the json module reads/writes JSON directly to and from Python dictionaries and lists.

items.title: pathlib Offers an Object-Oriented Alternative
items.text: Path objects from the pathlib module represent file paths as objects with methods (.exists(), .read_text(), .parent) rather than plain strings manipulated with os.path functions.

sections.title: How File Handling Actually Works — Modes, with, and the Errors They Explain

blocks.text: Three things separate someone who's copied a basic open()/read() snippet from someone who genuinely understands file handling: knowing exactly what each mode string does, understanding precisely why with is a correctness tool and not just a style choice, and recognising the specific errors that come from mismatched modes or missing files.
🔤 File Modes — What Each Letter Actually Does

'r' (read, the default if omitted) opens an existing file for reading and fails with FileNotFoundError if it doesn't exist. 'w' (write) creates a new file, or — importantly — completely overwrites an existing file's content with nothing, the instant it's opened, before you've even written anything. 'a' (append) opens the file for writing, but positions the cursor at the END, adding new content after whatever's already there rather than erasing it. 'x' (exclusive creation) creates a new file but raises FileExistsError if a file with that name already exists — useful specifically when you want to guarantee you're not silently overwriting something. Appending 'b' to any of these ('rb', 'wb') switches from text mode to binary mode, returning bytes objects instead of decoded str text — required for images, PDFs, or any non-text file.
⚠️ The Mode Mistake That Silently Destroys Data

This is the single most consequential file-handling mistake, and it doesn't raise an error at all — it just quietly, silently erases data. Opening a file with 'w' mode when you actually meant 'a' (or meant to read it first) instantly truncates the existing file to zero bytes, the moment open() succeeds, regardless of whether you go on to write anything at all. There's no confirmation prompt, no warning — the previous content is simply gone. I've genuinely lost data this way once, early on, opening a log file with 'w' inside a loop that ran on every iteration, wiping the file back to empty every single time instead of appending. The fix was one letter.
🛡️ Why with Is a Correctness Guarantee, Not Just Cleaner Syntax

Writing f = open(path); ...code...; f.close() works fine exactly as long as nothing between the open and the close ever raises an exception. The moment something does — a KeyError from bad data, a network timeout mid-processing, anything — Python jumps straight to propagating that exception, skipping every line after the point of failure, including your f.close() call. The file stays open. with open(path) as f: fundamentally changes this: it's built on Python's context manager protocol, which guarantees the file's __exit__ method (which calls close() internally) runs no matter how the block is exited — normal completion, a return statement, or an unhandled exception. This is why every serious Python style guide, and essentially every code review, treats bare open() without with as something to flag.
💥 FileNotFoundError — The Exact Trigger

Opening a file that doesn't exist in read mode raises FileNotFoundError: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: 'data.txt'. This is almost always caused by one of two things: a genuine typo in the filename or path, or — very commonly — a path that's correct relative to where you expected the script to run, but wrong relative to where it actually ran from, since Python resolves relative paths against the current working directory at the moment the script executes, not the directory the script file itself lives in.

Simple rule to remember: always use with open(...), never bare open() without it. Double-check 'w' versus 'a' before running anything that touches a file you care about. Specify encoding='utf-8' explicitly for text files rather than relying on the platform default.
Each mode string produces genuinely different behaviour, and choosing the wrong one is exactly how data gets silently lost or a script crashes unexpectedly.

sections.title: File Handling — Python vs Other Languages

blocks.text: Python's approach to guaranteed resource cleanup, through with and context managers, is genuinely cleaner than the equivalent pattern in several widely-used languages.

rows: Callbacks/Promises don't auto-close; manual or stream-based cleanup

blocks.text: Here's my honestly opinionated take: Python's with statement, applied to file handling, is one of the cleanest solutions to the 'guaranteed cleanup' problem I've used across any language. Java's try-with-resources achieves the same correctness guarantee but needs more visible ceremony around it. C simply doesn't have a language-level answer at all — fclose() forgotten inside an early-return branch is a genuinely common, real bug in C code, precisely because nothing enforces it. Python's version reads almost like plain English — with open(...) as f: — while quietly doing something structurally important underneath.

sections.title: Advantages and Disadvantages of Python's File Handling

blocks.text: Python's file handling model is genuinely well-designed, but it still has sharp edges worth knowing about explicitly.

pros.title: Simple, Consistent API Across File Types
pros.text: The same open() function, with just a different mode string, handles text files, binary files, reading, writing, and appending — one consistent entry point for nearly everything.

pros.title: Genuine Resource-Safety via with
pros.text: The with statement provides an actual correctness guarantee for cleanup, not just a stylistic convention, protecting against forgotten close() calls even when exceptions occur.

pros.title: Multiple Reading Strategies for Different Needs
pros.text: Reading an entire small file at once, line by line for memory efficiency, or lazily via iteration all use the same file object, letting you pick the right approach for the file's size.

pros.title: Standard Library Covers Common Structured Formats
pros.text: csv and json modules handle two of the most common structured file formats correctly out of the box, including edge cases manual string splitting would get wrong.

pros.title: Explicit Text vs Binary Distinction Prevents Corruption
pros.text: Requiring 'b' explicitly for binary mode makes it clear, at the point of opening a file, whether you're working with decoded text or raw bytes — preventing accidental encoding-related corruption.

pros.title: pathlib Offers a Cleaner Modern Alternative for Paths
pros.text: Object-oriented Path manipulation (path / 'subfolder' / 'file.txt') is genuinely more readable than string concatenation or repeated os.path.join() calls.

cons.title: 'w' Mode Silently Destroys Existing Content
cons.text: Opening a file in write mode instantly truncates it, with zero warning or confirmation — a genuinely dangerous default for anyone who mixes up 'w' and 'a' even once.

cons.title: Encoding Issues Are Easy to Introduce Silently
cons.text: Omitting an explicit encoding= argument relies on the platform default, which can differ between Windows, macOS, and Linux, causing bugs that only appear when code runs on a different machine.

cons.title: Forgetting with Is Still Genuinely Common
cons.text: Despite with being the recommended pattern, bare open()/close() code still appears frequently in tutorials, older codebases, and quick scripts, carrying real risk of leaked file handles.

cons.title: Relative Path Confusion
cons.text: Relative file paths are resolved against the current working directory at runtime, not the script's own location, which trips up developers who assume the two are always the same.

cons.title: No Built-in File Locking for Concurrent Access
cons.text: Python's standard open() offers no cross-platform file locking mechanism out of the box, meaning concurrent read/write access from multiple processes needs extra libraries or careful design.

cons.title: readlines() Can Consume Large Amounts of Memory
cons.text: Loading an entire large file into memory at once via .read() or .readlines() can be genuinely problematic for very large files, where line-by-line iteration is the safer, more scalable choice.

blocks.text: Line-by-Line Explanation

items.html: with open("notes.txt", "w", ...) as f: — 'w' creates the file if it doesn't exist, or truncates it to empty first if it does — every run of this specific block starts from a clean slate.
with open("notes.txt", "a", ...) as f: — 'a' opens with the cursor at the END of existing content, so this new write is added AFTER the two lines from the previous block, not replacing them.
for line in f: — Iterates over the file object directly, reading one line at a time. This is memory-efficient because it never loads the whole file into memory at once, unlike f.read().

csv.DictWriter and newline="" — The csv module correctly handles a comma embedded inside a field value like "Pune, MH" by quoting it in the output, something manual string joining with commas would get wrong. newline="" prevents the csv module from writing extra blank lines on Windows.

json.dump(data, f, indent=2) — Converts the Python dictionary directly into JSON text and writes it to the file in one call, with indent=2 producing nicely formatted, human-readable output rather than one dense line.

sections.title: Where File Handling Actually Matters — Real-World Applications

blocks.text: File handling isn't a standalone topic that stays in a textbook — it's woven into nearly every category of real Python program:

items.text: — Applications routinely read settings from a config file at startup (JSON, YAML, or .ini format), letting behaviour be changed without editing the actual source code — a genuinely standard pattern across scripts and full applications alike.

— Reading a CSV export from a spreadsheet or database, processing it, and writing results back out to a new file is one of the most common practical file-handling tasks in data-focused Python work, often paired with the pandas library for larger datasets.

— Writing timestamped log entries to a file, typically in append mode, is standard practice for tracking what a long-running script or service actually did, especially useful for diagnosing issues after the fact.

— Saving the result of an expensive API call to a local JSON file avoids re-fetching the same data repeatedly, a common pattern in scripts that would otherwise hit rate limits or slow external services unnecessarily.
— Downloading and saving images, PDFs, or other binary content requires opening files in binary mode ('wb'/'rb'), correctly handling raw bytes rather than decoded text.

— Automated test suites frequently read sample input files and compare processing results against expected output files, making reliable, predictable file handling a genuine prerequisite for trustworthy testing.
— Scripts that periodically export data from a database or application into files (for backup, sharing, or archival) rely directly on correct write and append handling to avoid data loss.

— Combined with the os or pathlib modules for listing directory contents, file handling scripts commonly loop through many files in a folder, applying the same read/process/write logic to each one automatically.

sections.title: Why File Handling Deserves Genuine, Careful Attention

blocks.text: File handling looks simple enough that it's tempting to treat it as a minor topic, but the consequences of getting it wrong are genuinely higher than most beginner topics. Here's why it's worth real attention:

items.strong: 💾 Mistakes Here Can Genuinely Destroy Data
items.text: — Unlike most beginner bugs that just produce a wrong number or an error message, a misused 'w' mode can permanently erase real content with zero warning — the stakes for getting this right are simply higher than most early topics.

items.strong: 🛡️ It's the Clearest Real-World Case for Context Managers
items.text: — Understanding exactly why with matters for files builds a genuinely transferable mental model for Python's broader context manager protocol, which shows up again with database connections, network sockets, and locks.

items.strong: 💼 It's a Practical Skill Tested in Real-World Coding Assessments
items.text: — Take-home coding tests and practical interview exercises frequently involve reading a data file and processing it — genuine file-handling fluency, not just theoretical knowledge, gets tested directly.

items.strong: 🌍 Encoding Bugs Are a Genuine, Recurring Real-World Problem
items.text: — Text encoding issues that only surface when code runs on a different machine or operating system are a real, documented category of production bugs — understanding encoding= explicitly is a practical, not academic, skill.

items.strong: 📊 It's Foundational for Data Science and Automation Work
items.text: — Nearly every data-focused or automation-focused Python task starts with reading input from somewhere and ends with writing output somewhere — file handling is genuinely the connective tissue of that entire category of work.

items.strong: 🇮🇳 It's a Standard, Practical Topic in Indian Data Analyst and Backend Interviews
items.text: — Practical exercises involving reading a CSV, processing it, and writing results are common in Indian data analyst and junior backend developer interview and assignment rounds, precisely because they test genuine, applied competence.

sections.title: pathlib and Modern File Handling Practices

blocks.text: Beyond the basic open() function, a few modern patterns and standard library tools are worth knowing for writing genuinely robust file-handling code.

items.text: — from pathlib import Path; p = Path('data') / 'users.csv' builds cross-platform-correct paths using the / operator, avoiding manual string concatenation and platform-specific separator issues entirely.

— Checking whether a file exists before attempting to open it, rather than relying purely on catching FileNotFoundError, is sometimes clearer for control flow, though catching the exception remains the more Pythonic approach for many cases (easier to ask forgiveness than permission).

— Convenience methods that handle opening, reading/writing, and closing a text file in a single call — Path('notes.txt').read_text(encoding='utf-8') is a compact alternative to the full with open(...) as f: pattern for simple cases.
— Creating necessary parent directories before writing a file into a path that might not fully exist yet — a common real-world need when generating output files into a fresh directory structure.

— Copying, moving, and deleting entire files or directory trees are handled by the shutil module rather than open(), since these are whole-file operations rather than content-reading/writing operations.

— When a script needs a scratch file that shouldn't persist, the tempfile module creates properly isolated, automatically-cleaned-up temporary files and directories rather than manually managing a file in a fixed, potentially-colliding location.

blocks.text: These come up regularly in Python interviews, especially for roles involving data processing, automation, or backend work.

items.q: Q1. What is the difference between 'w' and 'a' file modes in Python?
items.a: 'w' (write) mode creates a new file if it doesn't exist, or immediately truncates an existing file to empty the moment it's opened, before any writing has actually happened. 'a' (append) mode also creates a new file if needed, but if the file already exists, it opens with the cursor positioned at the END of the existing content, so new writes are added after what's already there rather than replacing it.

items.q: Q2. Why is using the with statement recommended over manually calling open() and close()?
items.a: The with statement, built on Python's context manager protocol, guarantees that a file's close() method runs automatically when the block exits — whether it exits normally or because an exception was raised partway through. A manual f.close() written after your code has no such guarantee: if an exception occurs before that line runs, close() simply never executes, leaving the file open.

items.q: Q3. What causes FileNotFoundError in Python, and how would you handle it gracefully?
items.a: FileNotFoundError is raised when attempting to open a file in read mode ('r') that doesn't exist at the specified path — commonly caused by a typo in the filename, or a relative path that's incorrect relative to the script's actual working directory at runtime. It's typically handled with a try/except FileNotFoundError block around the open() call, allowing the program to respond gracefully (create the file, prompt the user, or log the issue) instead of crashing.

items.q: Q4. What is the difference between .read(), .readline(), and .readlines() in Python file handling?
items.a: f.read() reads the entire file's contents into a single string. f.readline() reads just one line at a time, advancing the file's cursor position with each call. f.readlines() reads the entire file but returns a list of individual line strings, rather than one combined string. Iterating directly over the file object (for line in f:) is generally preferred over readlines() for large files, since it reads lazily rather than loading everything into memory at once.

items.q: Q5. Why does f.write('hello') not automatically add a newline, unlike print('hello')?
items.a: write() is a low-level operation that writes exactly the string it's given, with no automatic formatting added. print() specifically appends a newline character by default as part of its own convenience behaviour. When writing multiple lines to a file, you must explicitly include \n in each write() call, or join your lines with newlines before writing them as one combined string.

items.q: Q6. What is the difference between text mode and binary mode when opening a file in Python?
items.a: Text mode (the default, or explicitly 'r'/'w') automatically decodes the file's raw bytes into a Python str using a specified or platform-default text encoding, and encodes strings back to bytes when writing. Binary mode ('rb', 'wb') performs no decoding or encoding at all, working directly with raw bytes objects — required for non-text files like images, PDFs, or executables, where interpreting the content as text would corrupt it.

items.q: Q7. Why is it recommended to explicitly specify encoding='utf-8' when opening text files in Python?
items.a: Without an explicit encoding argument, open() uses the operating system's default text encoding, which can genuinely differ between platforms — for example, Windows often defaults to a different encoding than Linux or macOS. This can cause a script that works correctly on one machine to fail, or silently produce garbled text, when run on another. Explicitly specifying encoding='utf-8' ensures consistent, predictable behaviour regardless of the platform the code runs on.

items.q: Q8. How would you safely write JSON data to a file and read it back in Python?
items.a: Use the json module: json.dump(data, file_object) writes a Python dictionary or list directly to an already-open file as JSON text, and json.load(file_object) reads JSON text from an open file and parses it back into the corresponding Python dictionary or list. Both should be used inside a with open(...) as f: block to ensure the file is properly closed after the operation completes.

blocks.text: Work through these before checking the answers. Predicting exactly what ends up in a file — not just whether code runs without error — is the real test here.

items.q: 1. What happens to the existing content of data.txt (which currently contains 'old content') after running: with open('data.txt', 'w') as f: pass — with nothing written inside the block at all?
items.a: The file becomes completely empty. Simply opening a file in 'w' mode immediately truncates its existing content to zero bytes, regardless of whether anything is subsequently written — even an empty with block that does nothing else still erases the file's previous content.

items.q: 2. What is the output of a file after running: with open('log.txt', 'w') as f: f.write('Line 1') \n f.write('Line 2') — assuming the file is then read back?
items.a: 'Line 1Line 2' — as one single line, with no line break between them. write() never adds a newline automatically, so without an explicit \n included in the string, the two writes are simply concatenated directly together.

items.q: 3. What error occurs, and why, if you run: with open('report.txt', 'r') as f: content = f.read() — when report.txt has never been created?
items.a: FileNotFoundError: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: 'report.txt'. Opening a file in read mode ('r') requires the file to already exist; Python has no default file to fall back on and raises this specific exception immediately when open() is called.

items.q: 4. Why would with open('big_file.txt', 'r') as f: lines = f.readlines() potentially be a poor choice for a genuinely very large file, and what's the better alternative?
items.a: readlines() loads the ENTIRE file into memory at once as a list of every line, which can consume a large, possibly problematic amount of memory for a genuinely large file (multiple gigabytes, for instance). The better alternative is iterating directly over the file object — for line in f: — which reads and processes one line at a time, never holding the whole file in memory simultaneously.

items.q: 5. What does f.tell() return immediately after opening a file in 'r' mode and calling f.read() once on a 100-character file?
items.a: 100. tell() reports the current cursor position within the file, in bytes (or characters, for text mode with certain encodings). After reading the entire 100-character file with a single .read() call, the cursor has advanced all the way to the end, so tell() reports position 100.

items.q: 6. What's the bug in this code, and what does it actually do? for filename in ['a.txt', 'b.txt', 'c.txt']: with open('combined.txt', 'w') as f: f.write(open(filename).read())
items.a: Opening 'combined.txt' with 'w' mode INSIDE the loop truncates it on every single iteration, so the final result only contains the content of c.txt (the last file processed) — the content from a.txt and b.txt gets overwritten and lost. Also, open(filename) inside f.write() is never explicitly closed, leaking a file handle each iteration. The fix is opening 'combined.txt' with 'a' mode, or better, opening it once with 'w' OUTSIDE the loop, before iterating over the source files.

items.q:
7. What is the output of: import json 
 data = {'active': True, 'count': 3} 
 with open('x.json', 'w') as f: json.dump(data, f) 
 with open('x.json', 'r') as f: result = json.load(f) 
 print(type(result['active']))
items.a: <class 'bool'>. json.dump() correctly serialises Python's True to JSON's true, and json.load() correctly deserialises it back into a genuine Python bool object, not a string — the json module handles this type conversion faithfully in both directions.

items.q: 8. Why might code that works correctly when run directly (python script.py) raise FileNotFoundError when the exact same script is triggered from a different directory or by a scheduling tool like cron?
items.a: A relative file path like open('data.txt') is resolved against the CURRENT WORKING DIRECTORY at the moment the script actually runs, not the directory where the script file itself is saved. If the script is launched from a different location — a different terminal directory, or a cron job with a different working directory — that same relative path may no longer point to the intended file. The fix is typically using an absolute path, or building a path relative to the script's own location using __file__ and pathlib.

sections.title: Conclusion — Small Mistakes Here Have Real Consequences

blocks.text: File handling is deceptively simple-looking Python — three or four lines cover the common case — but it's one of the few beginner topics where a genuinely small mistake, a single wrong letter in a mode string, can cause real, permanent, unrecoverable damage to actual data. That's worth taking seriously, not as a scare tactic, but as an honest description of why this topic deserves more careful attention than its simple syntax might suggest.

If you're a complete beginner, the priority is building the with open(...) as f: pattern into pure muscle memory, to the point where writing bare open() without it feels visibly wrong. If you're doing real, production-adjacent work, the priority shifts to precision: explicit encoding, careful mode selection, and knowing exactly which standard library tool — csv, json, pathlib, plain open() — fits the specific file format and task in front of you.

rows: ✅ with open(...) as f: — never bare open()
✅ 'r' mode — but confirm the file actually exists first if uncertain
Adding new content without erasing old
✅ Iterate line by line, avoid .read() or .readlines() loading it all at once
✅ The csv module — never manual string splitting on commas
Any text file, on any platform
✅ Explicit encoding='utf-8', never rely on the platform default

blocks.text: The habit worth building here: before running any script that opens a file in 'w' mode, pause for one extra second and confirm — genuinely, deliberately — that overwriting that specific file's content is exactly what you intend. That single habit prevents the one file-handling mistake in this entire topic that can't be undone by re-running the script.

File handling rewards care precisely because the cost of carelessness is real. Use with every time, choose your mode deliberately, and be explicit about encoding — everything else about reading and writing files in Python follows naturally from those three habits. 🐍

items.q: How do I open and read a file in Python?
items.a: Use the built-in open() function inside a with statement: with open('filename.txt', 'r') as f: content = f.read(). The 'r' mode opens the file for reading, and using with ensures the file is automatically and safely closed once the block finishes, even if an error occurs while reading it.

items.q: What is the difference between 'w' and 'a' modes when opening a file in Python?
items.a: 'w' (write) mode immediately erases any existing content in the file the moment it's opened, starting fresh. 'a' (append) mode instead opens the file with the cursor positioned at the end of any existing content, so new writes are added after what's already there rather than replacing it. Mixing these up is a common cause of accidentally losing existing file content.

items.q: Why should I use the with statement when working with files in Python?
items.a: The with statement guarantees that a file gets closed automatically once the block finishes, whether it completes normally or an exception is raised partway through. Manually calling open() followed by close() offers no such guarantee — if an error occurs between those two calls, the close() line never runs, leaving the file open longer than intended.

items.q: Why do I get FileNotFoundError when trying to open a file in Python?
items.a: This error occurs when you try to open a file in read mode ('r') and Python can't find a file at the exact path specified — usually caused by a typo in the filename, or a relative path that doesn't point where you expect it to, since relative paths are resolved against the script's current working directory at runtime, not the folder the script file is saved in.

items.q: How do I read and write JSON files in Python?
items.a: Use the built-in json module: json.dump(data, file_object) writes a Python dictionary or list to an already-open file as JSON text, and json.load(file_object) reads JSON text from an open file and converts it back into a Python dictionary or list. Both are typically used inside a with open(...) as f: block to ensure proper file closing.

items.q: Should I specify an encoding when opening text files in Python?
items.a: Yes, it's genuinely recommended. Explicitly writing open(path, 'r', encoding='utf-8') ensures consistent, predictable text decoding regardless of which operating system the code runs on. Omitting the encoding argument relies on the platform's default encoding, which can differ between systems and cause subtle bugs that only appear when the same code runs on a different machine.
